The Speaker of the House of Representatives, Tajudeen Abbas, has acknowledged the economic hardship confronting Nigerians, describing the ongoing reforms of President Bola Tinubu’s administration as difficult but necessary to address longstanding structural weaknesses in the economy. Abbas, however, said the Federal Government must ensure that the benefits of the reforms translate into tangible improvements in the living conditions of ordinary Nigerians. The Speaker spoke on Monday during a panel session titled “Misinformation and Social Cohesion: Rebuilding Trust through Responsible Public Relations” at the Global Alliance World Public Relations Forum in Abuja. He was represented at the event by the House Majority Leader, Prof. Julius Ihonvbere. The forum brought together communication experts, public relations practitioners and global industry leaders to examine the changing responsibilities of the profession amid the growing influence of digital technology and the spread of misinformation. Acknowledging the economic difficulties facing the country, Abbas said the challenges confronting households and businesses were real and deserved serious attention. According to him, the economic situation should also be understood against the backdrop of global economic pressures and longstanding structural weaknesses in Nigeria’s economy. He said, “The difficulties confronting households and businesses are real and deserve serious attention. These difficulties must also be understood within the wider context of global economic pressures and long-standing structural weaknesses in our national economy. The challenge before government is to ensure that their benefits translate into tangible improvements in the lives of ordinary Nigerians.” Tinubu announced the removal of the petrol subsidy in his inaugural address on May 29, 2023, shortly after taking office. The government subsequently harmonised and floated the foreign exchange market, triggering significant adjustments in petrol prices and exchange rates, with consequential effects on the cost of living and doing business. Abbas said the government must also address the country’s security challenges through sustained action, accountability and stronger security institutions. Every innocent life lost today is a tragedy that calls for justice and accountability. “We must remain resolute in confronting those responsible, strengthening our security institutions, and protecting every Nigerian, irrespective of religion, ethnicity, or place of origin,” he said. The Speaker also highlighted the role of the National Assembly in strengthening democratic institutions, promoting accountability and addressing the country’s developmental challenges. He said the House of Representatives, through its 360 members, had a responsibility to ensure that the interests and concerns of Nigerians were reflected in national decision-making. Abbas said the House had pursued an eight-point legislative agenda covering good governance, national security, economic growth and development, education, healthcare, social inclusion, institutional strengthening and an open Parliament. He listed the proposed establishment of state police and the Reserved Seats for Women Bill among the constitutional and legislative initiatives being pursued by the House. Earlier in his speech, the Chairman, Senate Committee on Capital Market, Senator Osita Isiguzo, called for the regulation of artificial intelligence, warning that the technology could become dangerous if its misuse was left unchecked. Isiguzo said although AI offered significant opportunities, its capacity to generate convincing images and other forms of manipulated content posed a threat to information integrity. “AI is a major issue right now, and you know, globally, AI is not regulated in most climes just like when new media started, most jurisdictions did not find it necessary to regulate the new media except now that we are now saying, no, we cannot allow our children to have access to all manner of social media platforms. But we started late. “As a parliamentarian, I’m also of the opinion that AI must be regulated before AI will destroy the world,” he said. He added, “Now, when you see AI images, they look so real that sometimes you might not be able to discover which is AI and which is real. Don’t get me wrong, AI is good, but it has to be regulated before the goodness of AI becomes the calamity of the world.” Also speaking, the President and Chief Executive Officer, Global Alliance for Public Relations and Communication Management, Prof. Justin Green, highlighted the growing representation of Africa in the organisation’s leadership.
